data.text: Light from displays reaches the retina guided by both headset and eye lenses. Knowledge of light propagation and physics is key to understanding VR headset function, modeling virtual worlds, and determining rendering. Furthermore, understanding these systems along with camera mechanics helps with camera setup, panoramic videos, and building tracking hardware and software.
points: Light from displays reaches the retina guided by headset and eye lenses.
Understanding light through these lenses is key to VR headset function and perception.
Light propagation physics is used to model virtual worlds and determine rendering.
Understanding light, lenses, eyes, and cameras informs camera setup and panoramic videos.
Understanding camera mechanics helps build tracking hardware and software.

data.text: Light can be described by three views: the photon, wave, and ray views. The photon view describes light as energy particles useful for calculating light received by sensors, while the wave view describes light as ripples that help explain the color spectrum. Finally, the ray view describes light as trajectories to explain how lenses work and the concept of visibility.
points: Light can be described by the photon, wave, and ray views.
The photon view describes light as energy particles and is useful for calculating light received by sensors.
The wave view describes light as ripples and helps explain the color spectrum.
The ray view describes light as trajectories and is useful for explaining lenses and visibility.

data.text: When light rays strike a surface, they can be transmitted, absorbed, or reflected. Transmission occurs when light passes through a material, while absorption happens when light terminates inside it. Reflection occurs when light bounces off a surface without entering it.
points: Light rays can interact with surfaces through transmission, absorption, and reflection.
Transmission occurs when light rays pass through a material.
Absorption occurs when light rays terminate inside a material.
Reflection occurs when light rays bounce off a surface without entering it.

data.text: The perceived color of a surface point is determined by the intensity of the light reaching the viewer's eye. This includes ambient light from the environment, which is reflected from surrounding objects and reaches the eye together with light reflected from the object's surface.
points: The perceived color of a surface point is determined by the intensity of the light reaching the viewer's eye.
Ambient light reaches the viewer's eye together with light reflected from the object's surface.

data.text: Light enters the eye and is refracted by the cornea and lens to focus on the retina, where it is processed by rods and cones. Cones are primarily located in the central fovea to provide color and image acuity during photopic vision, while rods are more numerous in the periphery to aid sensitivity during scotopic vision.
points: Light passes through the cornea, pupil, and lens, which refract the light to focus it on the retina.
The retina contains two types of photoreceptors: rods, which are more numerous in the periphery, and cones, which are mainly in the central fovea.
Rods share optic nerve fibers to aid sensitivity to lower light levels, whereas each cone has its own fiber to aid image acuity.
Photopic vision uses cones for central color vision, while scotopic vision uses rods for peripheral vision in weak light.

data.text: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength. Visible light waves can excite cones in the eye, producing photopic vision, which is color perception. Light waves outside the visible light spectrum cannot excite cones and therefore do not produce color perception.
points: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies and wavelengths ranging from red to violet light.
Visible light waves excite cones in the eye to produce photopic vision, which is color perception.

data.text: Human eyes support central and peripheral vision because photoreceptor density varies across the retina. Central vision requires the eyes to be focused on the fovea to perceive sharp color images, while peripheral vision is supported by regions with lower photoreceptor density and is better at detecting movement. The blind spot is a region with no photoreceptors where visual stimuli produce no perception.
points: Human eyes support central and peripheral vision because photoreceptor density varies across the retina.
Central vision requires the eyes to be focused on the fovea to perceive sharp color images.
Peripheral vision is supported by regions with lower photoreceptor density and is better at detecting movement.
The blind spot is a region with no photoreceptors where visual stimuli produce no perception.
